questions.question: The magnetic moments associated with two closely wound circular coils A and B of radius $r_{A} = 10$ cm and $r_{B} = 20$ cm respectively are equal if : (Where $N_{A}, I_{A}$ and $N_{B}, I_{B}$ are number of turn and current of A and B respectively)
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The magnetic moment \(m\) of a circular coil is given by:

$$
m = IAN
$$

Where \(I\) is the current, \(A\) is the area of the coil, and \(N\) is the number of turns.

For coil A, with radius \(r_{A} = 10\) cm, current \(I_{A}\), and number of turns \(N_{A}\):

$$
m_{A} = I_{A} \pi r_{A}^2 N_{A}
$$

$$
m_{A} = I_{A} \pi N_{A} (10)^2
$$

$$
m_{A} = 100 \pi I_{A} N_{A} \quad \ldots(1)
$$

For coil B, with radius \(r_{B} = 20\) cm, current \(I_{B}\), and number of turns \(N_{B}\):

$$
m_{B} = I_{B} N_{B} \pi r_{B}^2
$$

$$
m_{B} = I_{B} N_{B} \pi (20)^2
$$

$$
m_{B} = 400 \pi I_{B} N_{B} \quad \ldots(2)
$$

Given that the magnetic moments are equal, \(m_{A} = m_{B}\):

$$
100 \pi I_{A} N_{A} = 400 \pi I_{B} N_{B}
$$

Divide both sides by \(100 \pi\):

$$
I_{A} N_{A} = 4 I_{B} N_{B}
$$

This matches option (3).

questions.question: Speed of an electron in Bohr's 7th orbit for Hydrogen atom is $3.6 \times 10^6$ m/s. The corresponding speed of the electron in 3rd orbit, in m/s is:
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

We know that the speed of an electron in Bohr's orbit for a hydrogen-like atom is given by the formula:

$$
V \propto \frac{Z}{n}
$$

For a Hydrogen atom, the atomic number \(Z = 1\). Therefore, the speed of the electron is inversely proportional to the principal quantum number (n):

$$
V \propto \frac{1}{n}
$$

This means that the ratio of speeds in two different orbits \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) is:

$$
\frac{V_1}{V_2} = \frac{n_2}{n_1}
$$

Given the speed of the electron in the 7th orbit (\(n_7 = 7\)) is \(V_7 = 3.6 \times 10^6\) m/s. We need to find the speed in the 3rd orbit (\(n_3 = 3\)), which is \(V_3\).

Using the proportionality relation:

$$
\frac{V_3}{V_7} = \frac{n_7}{n_3}
$$

Substitute the values of \(n_7\) and \(n_3\):

$$
\frac{V_3}{V_7} = \frac{7}{3}
$$

Now, substitute the given value of \(V_7\):

$$
V_3 = V_7 \times \frac{7}{3}
$$

$$
V_3 = (3.6 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}) \times \frac{7}{3}
$$

$$
V_3 = (\frac{3.6}{3} \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}) \times 7
$$

$$
V_3 = (1.2 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}) \times 7
$$

$$
V_3 = 8.4 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}
$$

questions.question: Heat is given to an ideal gas in an an isothermal process. • A. Internal energy of the gas will decrease. • B. Internal energy of the gas will increase. • C. Internal energy of the gas will not change. • D. The gas will do positive work. • E. The gas will do negative work. Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
In isothermal process

$$
\Delta T = 0
$$

So

$$
\Delta U = 0
$$

$$
\Delta Q = \omega + \Delta U
$$

$$
\boxed{\Delta Q = \omega}
$$

Since heat is given to the ideal gas, \(\Delta Q > 0\). Therefore, \(\omega > 0\), which means the gas will do positive work. Also, for an ideal gas in an isothermal process, the internal energy does not change.

So heat will be used to do positive work.

Thus, statements C (Internal energy of the gas will not change) and D (The gas will do positive work) are correct.

questions.question: A small object at rest, absorbs a light pulse of power 20 mW and duration 300 ns. Assuming speed of light as $3 \times 10^8$ m/s, the momentum of the object becomes equal to :
questions.explanation:
Power \(P = 20\) mW \(= 20 \times 10^{-3}\) W

Time duration \(t = 300\) ns \(= 300 \times 10^{-9}\) s

Speed of light \(C = 3 \times 10^8\) m/s

Energy absorbed \(E = P \times t\)

$$
E = (20 \times 10^{-3}) \times (300 \times 10^{-9})
$$

$$
E = 6000 \times 10^{-12} = 6 \times 10^{-9}\text{ J}
$$

For a completely absorbing surface, the momentum transferred is given by \(\Delta P = \frac{E}{C}\).

$$
\Delta P = \frac{6 \times 10^{-9}\text{ J}}{3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}}
$$

$$
\Delta P = 2 \times 10^{-17}\text{ kg m/s}
$$

Alternatively, we can use the concept of radiation pressure and force.

$$
\text{Pressure} = \frac{\text{Intensity}}{C} = \frac{\text{Power}}{\text{Area} \times C}
$$

$$
\text{Pressure} \times \text{Area} = \frac{\text{Power}}{C}
$$

$$
\text{Force} = \frac{\text{Power}}{C} = \frac{20 \times 10^{-3}}{3 \times 10^8}
$$

$$
F = \frac{20}{3} \times 10^{-11}\text{ N}
$$

The change in momentum \(\Delta P\) is equal to the impulse \(F \Delta t\).

$$
\Delta P = F \times t
$$

$$
\Delta P = \left(\frac{20}{3} \times 10^{-11}\right) \times (300 \times 10^{-9})
$$

$$
\Delta P = \frac{20 \times 300}{3} \times 10^{-11} \times 10^{-9}
$$

$$
\Delta P = 20 \times 100 \times 10^{-20}
$$

$$
\Delta P = 2000 \times 10^{-20} = 2 \times 10^3 \times 10^{-20}
$$

$$
\Delta P = 2 \times 10^{-17}\text{ kg m/s}
$$

questions.question: The pressure (P) and temperature (T) relationship of an ideal gas obeys the equation $PT^2 = \text{constant}$. The volume expansion coefficient of the gas will be :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

$$
PT^2 = \text{const.}
$$

$$
dV = V\gamma dT
$$

$$
\gamma = \frac{1}{V} \frac{dV}{dT} \quad ...(1)
$$

Using \(PV = nRT\) and \(PT^2 = \text{const.}\)

$$
\frac{nRT}{V} \cdot T^2 = \text{const}
$$

$$
V \propto T^3 \implies V = KT^3 \quad ...(2)
$$

Now put in (1)

$$
\gamma = \frac{1}{KT^3} \times 3KT^2 = \frac{3}{T} \implies \gamma = \frac{3}{T}
$$

questions.question: Two isolated metallic solid spheres of radii $R$ and $2R$ are charged such that both have same charge density $\sigma$. The spheres are then connected by a thin conducting wire. If the new charge density of the bigger sphere is $\sigma'$. The ratio $\frac{\sigma'}{\sigma}$ is :
questions.explanation:
Let the initial charge on the sphere with radius \(R\) be \(Q_1\) and on the sphere with radius \(2R\) be \(Q_2\). Since both have the same charge density \(\sigma\):

$$
Q_1 = \sigma \cdot (\text{Area of sphere 1}) = \sigma (4\pi R^2)
$$

$$
Q_2 = \sigma \cdot (\text{Area of sphere 2}) = \sigma (4\pi (2R)^2) = \sigma (16\pi R^2)
$$

When the spheres are connected by a thin conducting wire, charge will flow until the electric potential (voltage) of both spheres becomes equal. Let the new charges be \(Q_1'\) and \(Q_2'\) respectively.

The capacitance of a sphere of radius \(r\) is \(C = 4\pi\epsilon_0 r\).

$$
C_1 = 4\pi\epsilon_0 R
$$

$$
C_2 = 4\pi\epsilon_0 (2R)
$$

Since the potentials are equal, \(V_1' = V_2'\):

$$
\frac{Q_1'}{C_1} = \frac{Q_2'}{C_2}
$$

$$
\frac{Q_1'}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R} = \frac{Q_2'}{4\pi\epsilon_0 (2R)}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow 2Q_1' = Q_2' \quad \ldots(1)
$$

The total charge is conserved:

$$
Q_1 + Q_2 = Q_1' + Q_2'
$$

$$
\sigma (4\pi R^2) + \sigma (16\pi R^2) = Q_1' + Q_2'
$$

$$
\sigma (20\pi R^2) = Q_1' + Q_2'
$$

Substitute \(Q_2' = 2Q_1'\) from equation (1) into the conservation of charge equation:

$$
\sigma (20\pi R^2) = Q_1' + 2Q_1' = 3Q_1'
$$

$$
Q_1' = \frac{\sigma (20\pi R^2)}{3}
$$

$$
Q_2' = 2Q_1' = \frac{\sigma (40\pi R^2)}{3} \quad \ldots(2)
$$

The bigger sphere has radius \(2R\). Its new charge density is \(\sigma'\). The new charge \(Q_2'\) can also be expressed as:

$$
Q_2' = \sigma' \cdot (\text{Area of bigger sphere}) = \sigma' (4\pi (2R)^2) = \sigma' (16\pi R^2)
$$

Equating this with the expression for \(Q_2'\) from equation (2):

$$
\sigma' (16\pi R^2) = \frac{\sigma (40\pi R^2)}{3}
$$

Now, we need to find the ratio \(\frac{\sigma'}{\sigma}\):

$$
\frac{\sigma'}{\sigma} = \frac{40\pi R^2}{3 \cdot 16\pi R^2}
$$

$$
\frac{\sigma'}{\sigma} = \frac{40}{3 \cdot 16} = \frac{40}{48} = \frac{5}{6}
$$

questions.question: Choose the correct relationship between Poisson ratio ($\sigma$), bulk modulus (K) and modulus of rigidity ($\eta$) of a given solid object :
questions.explanation:
We know the relationships between Young's modulus (Y), bulk modulus (K), modulus of rigidity (\(\eta\)), and Poisson's ratio (\(\sigma\)) are:

$$
Y = 2\eta[1+\sigma]
$$

and

$$
Y = 3K[1-2\sigma]
$$

Equating the two expressions for Y:

$$
2\eta(1+\sigma) = 3K(1-2\sigma)
$$

Expand both sides:

$$
2\eta + 2\eta\sigma = 3K - 6K\sigma
$$

Group terms containing \(\sigma\) on one side and other terms on the other side:

$$
2\eta\sigma + 6K\sigma = 3K - 2\eta
$$

Factor out \(\sigma\):

$$
(2\eta + 6K)\sigma = 3K - 2\eta
$$

Solve for \(\sigma\):

$$
\sigma = \frac{3K - 2\eta}{2\eta + 6K}
$$

This matches option (2).

questions.question: In a screw gauge, there are 100 divisions on the circular scale and the main scale moves by 0.5 mm on a complete rotation of the circular scale. The zero of circular scale lies 6 divisions below the line of graduation when two studs are brought in contact with each other. When a wire is placed between the studs, 4 linear scale divisions are clearly visible while 46th division the circular scale coincide with the reference line. The diameter of the wire is _________ $\times 10^{-2}$ mm
questions.explanation:
Pitch = 0.5 mm

$$
L.C. = \frac{\text{pitch}}{\text{circular division}} = \frac{0.5 \text{mm}}{100} = 0.005 \text{mm}
$$

$$
\text{Zero error} = 6 \times \text{L.C.} = 6 \times (0.005) \text{ mm}
$$

$$
\text{Reading} = \text{main linear scale reading} + n(\text{L.C.}) - \text{zero error}
$$

$$
= 4(0.5 \text{mm}) + 46(0.005) - 6(0.005)
$$

$$
= 2 \text{ mm} + 40 \times 0.005 \text{ mm}
$$

$$
= 2 \text{ mm} + \frac{200}{1000} \text{ mm}
$$

$$
= 2.2 \text{ mm}
$$

$$
\text{Reading} = 220 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mm}
$$

questions.question:
Match Column-I with Column-II :
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

items.label: I
items.text: x-t graph showing an exponential decay curve, starting from x0 and approaching zero.

items.label: II
items.text: x-t graph showing a triangular shape, linear increase then linear decrease.

items.label: III
items.text: x-t graph showing a linear increase from origin with constant positive slope.

items.label: IV
items.text: v-t graph showing constant positive velocity, then zero velocity.

questions.explanation:
The velocity \(V\) is the derivative of position \(x\) with respect to time \(t\), i.e., \(V = \frac{dx}{dt}\). We need to find the slope of the x-t graph to determine the corresponding v-t graph.

The graph shows \(x \propto t^2\) (a parabola opening upwards). Taking the derivative:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt} \propto 2t \implies V \propto t
$$

This means velocity increases linearly with time, starting from zero. This matches with graph II.

The graph shows an exponential decay, which can be represented as \(x = x_0 e^{-\alpha t}\). Taking the derivative:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt} = x_0 e^{-\alpha t} (-\alpha) = -\alpha (x_0 e^{-\alpha t})
$$

So, \(V = -\alpha x_0 e^{-\alpha t}\). This means velocity is negative and its magnitude decreases exponentially with time, approaching zero. This matches with graph IV.

The graph shows a linear increase in position, then a linear decrease. This implies:

• For the increasing part: \(x \propto t\), so \(V = \text{constant (positive)}\).
• For the decreasing part: \(x \propto -t\), so \(V = \text{constant (negative)}\).

This matches with graph III, which shows a constant positive velocity followed by a constant negative velocity.

The graph shows a linear increase in position from the origin, meaning \(x \propto t\). Taking the derivative:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt} = \text{constant} \implies V = \text{constant (positive)}
$$

This matches with graph I, which shows a constant positive velocity, then zero velocity (assuming the linear part is for a specific duration).

Combining the matches: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I. This corresponds to option (4).

questions.question: A person has been using spectacles of power $-1.0$ dioptre for distant vision and a separate reading glass of power $2.0$ dioptres. What is the least distance of distinct vision for this person :
questions.explanation:
The power of the reading glass is given as \(P = 2.0\) dioptres. The focal length \(f\) can be calculated using the formula \(P = \frac{1}{f}\) (where \(f\) is in meters) or \(f = \frac{100}{P}\) (where \(f\) is in cm).

$$
f = \frac{100}{P} = \frac{100}{2.0} = 50 \text{ cm}
$$

For a person to read comfortably, the object (e.g., a book) is typically placed at the normal least distance of distinct vision, which is \(25\) cm. The reading glass forms a virtual image of this object at the person's actual near point. Let the person's least distance of distinct vision be \(x\).

According to the sign convention, the object distance \(u = -25\) cm (object is real and placed in front of the lens). The image formed by the reading glass is virtual and located at the person's near point, so \(v = -x\) (image is virtual and on the same side as the object).

Using the lens formula:

$$
\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{50} = \frac{1}{(-x)} - \frac{1}{(-25)}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{50} = -\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{25}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{x} = \frac{1}{25} - \frac{1}{50}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{x} = \frac{2}{50} - \frac{1}{50}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{x} = \frac{1}{50}
$$

$$
x = 50 \text{ cm}
$$

questions.question: The charge flowing in a conductor changes with time as $Q(t) = \alpha t - \beta t^2 + \gamma t^3$. Where $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are constants. Minimum value of current is :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Given the charge flowing in a conductor as a function of time:

$$
Q = \alpha t - \beta t^2 + \gamma t^3
$$

The current \(I\) is the rate of change of charge with respect to time, so we differentiate \(Q\) with respect to \(t\):

$$
I = \frac{dQ}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(\alpha t - \beta t^2 + \gamma t^3)
$$

$$
I = \alpha - 2\beta t + 3\gamma t^2
$$

To find the minimum value of current, we need to differentiate \(I\) with respect to \(t\) and set it to zero:

$$
\frac{dI}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(\alpha - 2\beta t + 3\gamma t^2)
$$

$$
\frac{dI}{dt} = 0 - 2\beta + 6\gamma t
$$

Set \(\frac{dI}{dt} = 0\) to find the time \(t\) at which the current is minimum:

$$
0 = -2\beta + 6\gamma t
$$

$$
6\gamma t = 2\beta
$$

$$
t = \frac{2\beta}{6\gamma} = \frac{\beta}{3\gamma}
$$

Now, substitute this value of \(t\) back into the expression for \(I\) to find the minimum current \(I_{\min}\):

$$
I_{\min} = \alpha - 2\beta\left(\frac{\beta}{3\gamma}\right) + 3\gamma\left(\frac{\beta}{3\gamma}\right)^2
$$

$$
I_{\min} = \alpha - \frac{2\beta^2}{3\gamma} + 3\gamma\left(\frac{\beta^2}{9\gamma^2}\right)
$$

$$
I_{\min} = \alpha - \frac{2\beta^2}{3\gamma} + \frac{3\gamma\beta^2}{9\gamma^2}
$$

$$
I_{\min} = \alpha - \frac{2\beta^2}{3\gamma} + \frac{\beta^2}{3\gamma}
$$

$$
I_{\min} = \alpha - \frac{\beta^2}{3\gamma}
$$

This matches option (3).

questions.question: Electric field in a certain region is given by $\vec{E} = \left(\frac{A}{x^2}\hat{i} + \frac{B}{y^3}\hat{j}\right)$ The SI unit of A and B are :
questions.explanation:
The electric field \(\vec{E}\) has units of Newtons per Coulomb (N/C).

$$
\vec{E} = \frac{A}{x^2}\hat{i} + \frac{B}{y^3}\hat{j}
$$

For the first term, \(\frac{A}{x^2}\) must have units of N/C.

Unit of \(A\) = Unit of \(E\) \(\times\) Unit of \(x^2\)

$$
\text{Unit of A} = \frac{N}{C} \times m^2 = Nm^2C^{-1}
$$

For the second term, \(\frac{B}{y^3}\) must also have units of N/C.

Unit of \(B\) = Unit of \(E\) \(\times\) Unit of \(y^3\)

$$
\text{Unit of B} = \frac{N}{C} \times m^3 = Nm^3C^{-1}
$$

Thus, the SI unit of A is \(Nm^2C^{-1}\) and the SI unit of B is \(Nm^3C^{-1}\).

Using De Morgan's theorem, \(\overline{X \cdot Y} = \overline{X} + \overline{Y}\) and \(\overline{\overline{X}} = X\) .

So, \(Y = \overline{\overline{A}} + \overline{\overline{B}}\) which simplifies to \(Y = A + B\) .

Therefore, the given logical circuit is equivalent to an OR gate.

questions.question: A sinusoidal carrier voltage is amplitude modulated. The resultant amplitude modulated wave has maximum and minimum amplitude of 120 V and 80 V respectively. The amplitude of each sideband is :
questions.explanation:
Given:

$$
V_{\text{max}} = 120 \text{ V}
$$

$$
V_{\text{min}} = 80 \text{ V}
$$

For an amplitude modulated wave, the maximum and minimum amplitudes are given by:

$$
V_{\text{max}} = V_c + V_m \quad \dots(1)
$$

$$
V_{\text{min}} = V_c - V_m \quad \dots(2)
$$

Substitute the given values into the equations:

$$
120 = V_c + V_m \quad \dots(1)
$$

$$
80 = V_c - V_m \quad \dots(2)
$$

Adding equation (1) and (2):

$$
(V_c + V_m) + (V_c - V_m) = 120 + 80
$$

$$
2V_c = 200
$$

$$
V_c = 100 \text{ V}
$$

Substitute the value of \(V_c\) into equation (1) to find \(V_m\):

$$
120 = 100 + V_m
$$

$$
V_m = 120 - 100
$$

$$
V_m = 20 \text{ V}
$$

The modulation index (\(\mu\)) is given by the ratio of the modulating signal amplitude to the carrier amplitude:

$$
\mu = \frac{V_m}{V_c}
$$

$$
\mu = \frac{20}{100} = 0.2
$$

The amplitude of each sideband (upper sideband or lower sideband) is given by:

$$
A_{\text{sideband}} = \frac{\mu V_c}{2}
$$

Substitute the values of \(\mu\) and \(V_c\):

$$
A_{\text{sideband}} = \frac{0.2 \times 100}{2}
$$

$$
A_{\text{sideband}} = \frac{20}{2}
$$

$$
A_{\text{sideband}} = 10 \text{ V}
$$

questions.question: A horse rider covers half the distance with 5 m/s speed. The remaining part of the distance was travelled with speed 10 m/s for half the time and with speed 15 m/s for other half of the time. The mean speed of the rider averaged over the whole time of motion is $\frac{x}{7}$ m/s. The value of $x$ is
questions.explanation:
Let the total distance be \(2D\). The first half of the distance, \(D\), is covered with a speed of \(5\) m/s. The remaining half of the distance, \(D\), is covered in two equal time intervals, say \(t\), with speeds \(10\) m/s and \(15\) m/s respectively.

For the second half of the journey (from B to D in the diagram), the distance is covered in two equal time intervals. The average speed for this part is the arithmetic mean of the speeds:

$$
V_{\mathrm{BD}} = \frac{10 + 15}{2} = \frac{25}{2} \text{ m/sec}
$$

Now, we have two segments of equal distance \(D\). The first segment is covered at \(5\) m/s. The second segment is covered at an average speed of \(\frac{25}{2}\) m/s. For two segments of equal distance, the average speed is given by the harmonic mean of the speeds:

$$
\frac{2}{V_{\mathrm{avg}}} = \frac{1}{V_1} + \frac{1}{V_2}
$$

Substituting the values:

$$
\frac{2}{V_{\mathrm{avg}}} = \frac{1}{5} + \frac{1}{\frac{25}{2}}
$$

$$
\frac{2}{V_{\mathrm{avg}}} = \frac{1}{5} + \frac{2}{25}
$$

$$
\frac{2}{V_{\mathrm{avg}}} = \frac{5}{25} + \frac{2}{25} = \frac{7}{25}
$$

$$
V_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{2 \times 25}{7} = \frac{50}{7} \text{ m/sec}
$$

The problem states that the mean speed is \(\frac{x}{7}\) m/s.

$$
\frac{x}{7} = \frac{50}{7}
$$

questions.question: A massless square loop, of wire of resistance $10\Omega$, supporting a mass of $1\ g$, hangs vertically with one of its sides in a uniform magnetic field of $10^3\ G$, directed outwards in the shaded region. A dc voltage $V$ is applied to the loop. For what value of $V$, the magnetic force will exactly balance the weight of the supporting mass of $1\ g$ ? (If sides of the loop = $10\ cm$, $g = 10\ ms^{-2}$)
questions.explanation:
For balancing \(\to\) \(l = 10\ cm = 0.1\ m\), \(B = 10^3\ G = 0.1\ T\), \(m = 1\ g = 10^{-3}\ kg\)

$$
F_m = mg
$$

$$
IlB = mg
$$

Substituting \(I = \frac{V}{R}\) and converting units:

$$
\frac{V}{R} (0.1)(0.1) = \frac{1}{1000} \times 10
$$

$$
\frac{V}{100R} = \frac{1}{100}
$$

Given \(R = 10\Omega\). Substituting \(R\):

$$
\frac{V}{10} = 1 \Rightarrow V = 10\ Volt
$$

questions.question: In Young's double slit experiment, two slits $S_1$ and $S_2$ are '$d$' distance apart and the separation from slits to screen is $D$ (as shown in figure). Now if two transparent slabs of equal thickness $0.1$ mm but refractive index $1.51$ and $1.55$ are introduced in the path of beam ($\lambda = 4000\mathring{A}$) from $S_1$ and $S_2$ respectively. The central bright fringe spot will shift by number of fringes.
questions.explanation:
Given values:

• \(\mu_1 = 1.51\)
• \(\mu_2 = 1.55\)
• \(t = 0.1\) mm
• \(\lambda = 4000\mathring{A}\)

The path difference \(\Delta x\) at point \(P\) on the screen is given by:

$$
\Delta x = [S_1P + (\mu_1 - 1)t] - [S_2P + (\mu_2 - 1)t]
$$

For the central maxima, the path difference \(\Delta x\) must be zero.

$$
0 = (S_1P - S_2P) + (\mu_1 - 1)t - (\mu_2 - 1)t
$$

The loss of energy \(\Delta U\) when two capacitors \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) with initial voltages \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) are connected in parallel is given by:

$$
\Delta U = \frac{1}{2} \frac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2} (V_1 - V_2)^2

In this case, \(C_1 = C\), \(C_2 = C\), \(V_1 = 100 V\), and \(V_2 = 0 V\) (since the second capacitor is uncharged).

$$

$$

questions.question: The general displacement of a simple harmonic oscillator is $x = A \sin \omega t$. Let $T$ be its time period. The slope of its potential energy (U) - time (t) curve will be maximum when $t = \frac{T}{\beta}$. The value of $\beta$ is
questions.explanation:
Given displacement:

$$
x = A \sin(\omega t)
$$

Potential energy of a simple harmonic oscillator is given by:

$$
U = \frac{1}{2} kx^2
$$

Substitute the expression for \(x\) into the potential energy equation:

$$
U = \frac{1}{2} K A^2 \sin^2 (\omega t)
$$

To find the slope of the potential energy-time curve, differentiate \(U\) with respect to \(t\):

$$
\frac{dU}{dt} = \frac{KA^2}{2} \cdot 2 \sin(\omega t) \cos(\omega t) \cdot \omega
$$

Using the trigonometric identity \(2 \sin A \cos A = \sin(2A)\), the slope becomes:

$$
\text{Slope} = \frac{dU}{dt} = \frac{\omega KA^2}{2} \sin(2\omega t)
$$

The slope will be maximum when \(\sin(2\omega t)\) is maximum. The maximum value of \(\sin(2\omega t)\) is 1, which occurs when:

$$
2\omega t = \frac{\pi}{2}
$$

We are given that the slope is maximum when \(t = \frac{T}{\beta}\). Also, we know that \(\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}\). Substitute these into the equation:

$$
2 \left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right) \left(\frac{T}{\beta}\right) = \frac{\pi}{2}
$$

Simplify the equation:

$$
\frac{4\pi}{\beta} = \frac{\pi}{2}
$$

Solve for \(\beta\):

$$
\beta = \frac{4\pi \cdot 2}{\pi}
$$

$$
\beta = 8
$$

questions.question: In a series LR circuit with $X_{L} = R$, power factor is $P_{1}$. If a capacitor of capacitance C with $X_{C} = X_{L}$ is added to the circuit the power factor becomes $P_{2}$. The ratio of $P_{1}$ to $P_{2}$ will be :
questions.explanation:
For a series LR circuit, the impedance \(Z\) is given by \(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + X_{L}^{2}}\). The power factor \(P\) is defined as \(\cos \phi = \frac{R}{Z}\).

Given that \(X_{L} = R\), the impedance for the LR circuit is:

$$
Z_{1} = \sqrt{R^{2} + X_{L}^{2}} = \sqrt{R^{2} + R^{2}} = \sqrt{2R^{2}} = R\sqrt{2}
$$

So, the power factor \(P_{1}\) is:

$$
P_{1} = \frac{R}{Z_{1}} = \frac{R}{R\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
$$

When a capacitor of capacitance C with \(X_{C} = X_{L}\) is added to the circuit, it becomes an LCR series circuit. The impedance \(Z\) for an LCR circuit is given by \(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_{L} - X_{C})^{2}}\).

Given that \(X_{C} = X_{L}\), the term \((X_{L} - X_{C})\) becomes zero. The impedance for the LCR circuit is:

$$
Z_{2} = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_{L} - X_{C})^{2}} = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_{L} - X_{L})^{2}} = \sqrt{R^{2} + 0} = R
$$

So, the power factor \(P_{2}\) is:

$$
P_{2} = \frac{R}{Z_{2}} = \frac{R}{R} = 1
$$

Now, we calculate the ratio \(\frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}}\):

$$
\frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}} = \frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}{1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
$$

questions.question: A point source of light is placed at the centre of curvature of a hemispherical surface. The source emits a power of 24 W. The radius of curvature of hemisphere is 10 cm and the inner surface is completely reflecting. The force on the hemisphere due to the light falling on it is ________ $10^{-8}$ N
questions.explanation:
The solution indicates the answer is 4.

For a completely reflecting surface, the angle of incidence is \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\).

The pressure due to reflecting surface is given by \(\frac{2I}{C}\).

$$
F_{\text{net}} = \frac{2I}{C} \times \text{Area} \quad ......(1)
$$

Now, intensity \(I\) is defined as power per unit area. For a point source emitting uniformly in all directions, the intensity at a distance \(r\) is:

$$
I = \frac{\text{Power}}{\text{Area}} = \frac{\text{Power}}{4\pi r^2}
$$

From equation (1), the net force is:

$$
F_{\text{net}} = \frac{2I}{C} \times \text{Projected Area}
$$

For a hemisphere, the projected area is \(\pi r^2\). Substituting the expression for \(I\):

$$
F_{\text{net}} = \frac{2}{C} \times \frac{\text{Power}}{4\pi r^2} \times \pi r^2
$$

Simplifying the expression:

$$
F_{\text{net}} = \frac{2 \times \text{Power}}{4C}
$$

Given: Power \(= 24\) W, speed of light \(C = 3 \times 10^8\) m/s.

$$
F_{\text{net}} = \frac{2 \times 24}{3 \times 10^8 \times 4}
$$

$$
F_{\text{net}} = \frac{48}{12 \times 10^8} = \frac{4}{10^8} = 4 \times 10^{-8} \text{ N}
$$

questions.question: If the gravitational field in the space is given as $ -\frac{K}{r^2} $. Taking the reference point to be at $r = 2$ cm with gravitational potential $V = 10$ J/kg. Find the gravitational potential at $r = 3$ cm in SI unit (Given, that $K = 6$ Jcm/kg )
questions.explanation:
The relation between gravitational potential difference and gravitational field is given by:

$$
\Delta V = - \int_{r_1}^{r_2} \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}
$$

Given \(E = -\frac{K}{r^2}\) and we need to find potential at \(r = 3\) cm, given potential at \(r = 2\) cm is \(10\) J/kg. Also, \(K = 6\) Jcm/kg. First, convert K to SI units:

$$
K = 6 \text{ Jcm/kg} = 6 \times 10^{-2} \text{ Jm/kg}
$$

The limits of integration are from \(r_1 = 2\) cm to \(r_2 = 3\) cm, which are \(0.02\) m and \(0.03\) m respectively.

$$
V(3) - V(2) = - \int_{0.02}^{0.03} \left( -\frac{K}{r^2} \right) dr
$$

$$
V(3) - V(2) = K \int_{0.02}^{0.03} \frac{1}{r^2} dr
$$

$$
V(3) - V(2) = K \left[ -\frac{1}{r} \right]_{0.02}^{0.03}
$$

$$
V(3) - V(2) = -K \left[ \frac{1}{0.03} - \frac{1}{0.02} \right]
$$

$$
V(3) - 10 = - (6 \times 10^{-2}) \left[ \frac{100}{3} - \frac{100}{2} \right]
$$

$$
V(3) - 10 = - (6 \times 10^{-2}) \left[ \frac{200 - 300}{6} \right]
$$

$$
V(3) - 10 = - (6 \times 10^{-2}) \left[ -\frac{100}{6} \right]
$$

$$
V(3) - 10 = (6 \times 10^{-2}) \times \frac{100}{6}
$$

$$
V(3) - 10 = 1
$$

$$
V(3) = 10 + 1
$$

$$
V(3) = 11 \text{ J/kg}
$$

questions.question: The figure represents the momentum time (p-t) curve for a particle moving along an axis under the influence of the force. Identify the regions on the graph where the magnitude of the force is maximum and minimum respectively ? If $(t_{3} - t_{2}) \lt t_{1}$
questions.explanation:
### Analysis of Momentum-Time Graph

The force acting on a particle is given by the rate of change of momentum with respect to time. Therefore, the slope of the momentum-time (p-t) curve represents the force.

$$
F = \frac{dP}{dt} = \text{slope}
$$

From the given graph, we need to identify the regions with maximum and minimum magnitude of slope.

• Region (a) has a positive slope.
• Region (b) has a smaller positive slope (least steep).
• Region (c) has a large negative slope (steepest).

The magnitude of the force is the absolute value of the slope.

• Maximum magnitude of slope \(\to\) region (c) (steepest slope, regardless of sign).
• Minimum magnitude of slope \(\to\) region (b) (least steep slope, closest to zero).

questions.question: A ball of mass 200 g rests on a vertical post of height 20 m. A bullet of mass 10 g, travelling in horizontal direction, hits the centre of the ball. After collision both travels independently. The ball hits the ground at a distance 30 m and the bullet at a distance of 120 m from the foot of the post. The value of initial velocity of the bullet will be (if $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$) :
questions.explanation:
Time to reach ground will be same for both the ball and the bullet, as they fall from the same height \(h = 20\text{ m}\) under gravity.

$$
t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 20}{10}} = \sqrt{4} = 2\text{ sec}
$$

For the bullet, range \(R_{\text{bullet}} = 120\text{ m}\). Its horizontal velocity after collision is \(v_2\).

$$
R_{\text{bullet}} = v_2 t \Rightarrow 120 = v_2 (2) \Rightarrow v_2 = 60\text{ m/sec}
$$

For the ball, range \(R_{\text{ball}} = 30\text{ m}\). Its horizontal velocity after collision is \(v_1\).

$$
R_{\text{ball}} = v_1 t \Rightarrow 30 = v_1 (2) \Rightarrow v_1 = 15\text{ m/sec}
$$

Now, we apply the principle of conservation of linear momentum in the horizontal direction just before and after the collision.

$$
P_{\text{initial}} = P_{\text{final}}
$$

$$
(m_{\text{ball}} v_{\text{ball, initial}}) + (m_{\text{bullet}} v_{\text{bullet, initial}}) = (m_{\text{ball}} v_{\text{ball, final}}) + (m_{\text{bullet}} v_{\text{bullet, final}})
$$

Given masses: \(m_{\text{ball}} = 200\text{ g} = 0.2\text{ kg}\) and \(m_{\text{bullet}} = 10\text{ g} = 0.01\text{ kg}\).

The ball is initially at rest, so \(v_{\text{ball, initial}} = 0\text{ m/s}\). Let the initial velocity of the bullet be \(v_0\).

$$
0 + (0.01)v_0 = (0.2)(15) + (0.01)(60)
$$

$$
0.01v_0 = 3 + 0.6
$$

$$
0.01v_0 = 3.6
$$

$$
v_0 = \frac{3.6}{0.01} = 360\text{ m/sec}
$$

questions.question: The height of liquid column raised in a capillary tube of certain radius when dipped in liquid A vertically is, 5 cm. If the tube is dipped in a similar manner in another liquid B of surface tension and density double the values of liquid A, the height of liquid column raised in liquid B would be m
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The height of a liquid column raised in a capillary tube is given by Jurin's Law:

$$
h = \frac{2T \cos \theta}{r \rho g}
$$

Where:

• \(h\) is the height of the liquid column
• \(T\) is the surface tension of the liquid
• \(\theta\) is the contact angle
• \(r\) is the radius of the capillary tube
• \(\rho\) is the density of the liquid
• \(g\) is the acceleration due to gravity

For a given capillary tube (constant \(r\)), and assuming the contact angle \(\theta\) and gravity \(g\) remain constant, the height \(h\) is directly proportional to the surface tension \(T\) and inversely proportional to the density \(\rho\).

$$
h \propto \frac{T}{\rho}
$$

Let \(h_1\), \(T_1\), \(\rho_1\) be the height, surface tension, and density for liquid A, and \(h_2\), \(T_2\), \(\rho_2\) for liquid B. We can write the ratio of heights as:

$$
\frac{h_2}{h_1} = \frac{T_2}{T_1} \times \frac{\rho_1}{\rho_2}
$$

Given:

• Height for liquid A, \(h_1 = 5\) cm
• Surface tension of liquid B is double that of liquid A: \(T_2 = 2T_1\)
• Density of liquid B is double that of liquid A: \(\rho_2 = 2\rho_1\)

Substitute these values into the ratio equation:

$$
\frac{h_2}{5\text{cm}} = \frac{2T_1}{T_1} \times \frac{\rho_1}{2\rho_1}
$$

$$
\frac{h_2}{5\text{cm}} = 2 \times \frac{1}{2}
$$

$$
\frac{h_2}{5\text{cm}} = 1
$$

$$
h_2 = 5\text{cm}
$$

To convert centimeters to meters, divide by 100:

$$
h_2 = \frac{5}{100}\text{m} = 0.05\text{m}
$$

questions.question: In an experiment for estimating the value of focal length of converging mirror, image of an object placed at 40 cm from the pole of the mirror is formed at distance 120 cm from the pole of the mirror. These distances are measured with a modified scale in which there are 20 small divisions in 1 cm. The value of error in measurement of focal length of the mirror is $\frac{1}{K}$ cm. The value of K is
questions.explanation:
The mirror formula is given by:

$$
\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}
$$

To find the error in focal length, we differentiate the mirror formula:

$$
f^{-1} = v^{-1} + u^{-1}
$$

$$
(-1)f^{-2}df = (-1)v^{-2}dv + (-1)u^{-2}du
$$

$$
\frac{df}{f^2} = \frac{dv}{v^2} + \frac{du}{u^2} \quad \ldots(1)
$$

Given values for object distance (u) and image distance (v) for a converging mirror:

$$
u = -40 \text{ cm}
$$

$$
v = -120 \text{ cm}
$$

Calculate the focal length (f):

$$
\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{-120} + \frac{1}{-40}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1 + 3}{-120} = \frac{4}{-120} = \frac{1}{-30}
$$

$$
f = -30 \text{ cm}
$$

The error in measurement for u and v (du, dv) is determined by the modified scale. 20 small divisions in 1 cm means each division is \(\frac{1}{20}\) cm. So, the least count or error is:

$$
du = dv = \frac{1 \text{ cm}}{20} = 0.05 \text{ cm}
$$

Now, substitute the values of f, u, v, du, and dv into equation (1):

$$
\frac{df}{(30)^2} = \frac{0.05}{(120)^2} + \frac{0.05}{(40)^2}
$$

$$
\frac{df}{900} = \frac{0.05}{14400} + \frac{0.05}{1600}
$$

$$
\frac{df}{900} = 0.05 \left( \frac{1}{14400} + \frac{1}{1600} \right)
$$

$$
\frac{df}{900} = 0.05 \left( \frac{1 + 9}{14400} \right)
$$

$$
\frac{df}{900} = 0.05 \left( \frac{10}{14400} \right)
$$

$$
\frac{df}{900} = \frac{0.5}{14400}
$$

$$
df = \frac{0.5 \times 900}{14400}
$$

$$
df = \frac{450}{14400} = \frac{45}{1440} = \frac{1}{32} \text{ cm}
$$

The problem states that the error in measurement of focal length is \(\frac{1}{K}\) cm.

$$
\frac{1}{K} = df
$$

$$
\frac{1}{K} = \frac{1}{32}
$$

$$
K = 32
$$

questions.question: In the following circuit, the magnitude of current $I_{1}$, is _______ A.
questions.explanation:
Let the voltage at junction A be \(V_{A} = x\) and at junction D be \(V_{D} = y\). We set the potential at junction C to \(V_{C} = 0\) V. From the circuit, the potential at junction B is \(V_{B} = 2\) V (due to the 2V cell).

The sum of currents leaving junction A is zero:

$$
\frac{V_{A} - V_{B}}{1\Omega} + \frac{V_{A} - V_{C}}{1\Omega} + \frac{V_{A} - (V_{D} - 5V)}{1\Omega} = 0
$$

$$
\frac{x - 2}{1} + \frac{x - 0}{1} + \frac{x + 5 - y}{1} = 0
$$

$$
3x - y + 3 = 0 \quad \text{...(1)}
$$

The sum of currents leaving junction D is zero:

$$
\frac{V_{D} - V_{C}}{2\Omega} + \frac{V_{D} - V_{B}}{2\Omega} + \frac{V_{D} - (V_{A} + 5V)}{1\Omega} = 0
$$

$$
\frac{y - 0}{2} + \frac{y - 2}{2} + \frac{y - x - 5}{1} = 0
$$

Multiplying by 2 to clear denominators:

$$
y + (y - 2) + 2(y - x - 5) = 0
$$

$$
y + y - 2 + 2y - 2x - 10 = 0
$$

$$
4y - 2x - 12 = 0
$$

$$
2y - x = 6 \quad \text{...(2)}
$$

We have a system of two linear equations:

• From (1): \(3x - y = -3\)
• From (2): \(-x + 2y = 6\)

Multiply equation (1) by 2:

$$
6x - 2y = -6 \quad \text{...(3)}
$$

Add equation (2) and (3):

$$
(-x + 2y) + (6x - 2y) = 6 + (-6)
$$

$$
5x = 0 \implies x = 0
$$

Substitute \(x = 0\) into equation (2):

$$
2y - 0 = 6 \implies 2y = 6 \implies y = 3
$$

So, the node potentials are \(V_{A} = x = 0\) V and \(V_{D} = y = 3\) V.

Current \(I_{1}\) is the current flowing upwards through the 2V cell, into junction B. Let's apply KCL at junction B. The currents entering junction B are \(I_{1}\) and \(I_{3}\). The current leaving junction B is the current flowing towards A through the \(1\Omega\) resistor.

Current \(I_{3}\) flows from D to B through the top \(2\Omega\) resistor. So, \(I_{3} = \frac{V_{D} - V_{B}}{2\Omega}\).

$$
I_{3} = \frac{y - 2}{2} = \frac{3 - 2}{2} = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5 \text{ A}
$$

Current from B to A is \(I_{BA} = \frac{V_{B} - V_{A}}{1\Omega}\).

$$
I_{BA} = \frac{2 - x}{1} = \frac{2 - 0}{1} = 2 \text{ A}
$$

Applying KCL at B: \(I_{1} + I_{3} = I_{BA}\)

$$
I_{1} + 0.5 = 2
$$

$$
I_{1} = 2 - 0.5 = 1.5 \text{ A}
$$

questions.question: A 300 mL bottle of soft drink has $0.2M\text{CO}_{2}$ dissolved in it. Assuming $\text{CO}_{2}$ behaves as an ideal gas, the volume of the dissolved $\text{CO}_{2}$ at STP is ______ mL. (Nearest integer) Given : At STP , molar volume of an ideal gas is $22.7 \text{ L mol}^{-1}$
questions.explanation:

questions.question: The number of electrons involved in the reduction of permanganate to manganese dioxide in acidic medium is

$$
x + 4(-2) = -1
$$

$$
x - 8 = -1
$$

$$
x = +7
$$

In manganese dioxide (\(MnO_{2}\)), oxygen has an oxidation state of -2. Let the oxidation state of manganese be \(y\).

$$
y + 2(-2) = 0
$$

$$
y - 4 = 0
$$

$$
y = +4
$$

The reduction of permanganate to manganese dioxide involves a change in the oxidation state of manganese from \(+7\) to \(+4\). The number of electrons gained is the difference between these oxidation states.

$$
\text{Number of electrons} = (+7) - (+4) = 3
$$

This means 3 electrons are gained during the reduction process.

The balanced half-reaction for the reduction of \(MnO_{4}^{-}\) to \(MnO_{2}\) in acidic medium is:

$$
4H^{+} + MnO_{4}^{-} + 3e^{-} \rightarrow MnO_{2} + 2H_{2}O

The equation clearly shows that 3 electrons (\(3e^{-}\)) are involved in the reduction.

questions.question: For $OF_{2}$ molecule consider the following : • A. Number of lone pairs on oxygen is 2. • B. FOF angle is less than $104.5^{\circ}$. • C. Oxidation state of O is $-2$. • D. Molecule is bent 'V' shaped. • E. Molecular geometry is linear. correct options are:
questions.explanation:
The central atom is Oxygen (O). Oxygen belongs to Group 16, so it has 6 valence electrons. It forms two single bonds with two Fluorine (F) atoms. Fluorine is more electronegative than Oxygen.

• **Number of lone pairs on Oxygen:** Total valence electrons around O = 6 (from O) + 2 (from 2F) = 8 electrons. Number of bond pairs = 2. Number of lone pairs = \((8 - 2 \times 2) / 2 = 2\). So, statement A is **correct**.
• **Oxidation state of O:** Since F is more electronegative than O, F has an oxidation state of -1. For \(OF_{2}\), the total charge from two F atoms is \(2 \times (-1) = -2\). To maintain neutrality, the oxidation state of O must be +2. So, statement C (Oxidation state of O is -2) is **incorrect**.
• **Steric number and geometry:** The steric number for O is 2 (bond pairs) + 2 (lone pairs) = 4. This corresponds to \(sp^{3}\) hybridization and a tetrahedral electron geometry. Due to the presence of two lone pairs, the molecular geometry is bent or V-shaped. So, statement D is **correct** and statement E (Molecular geometry is linear) is **incorrect**.
• **FOF bond angle:** The ideal tetrahedral angle is \(109.5^{\circ}\). However, due to lone pair-lone pair and lone pair-bond pair repulsions, the bond angle in \(OF_{2}\) is reduced. The actual bond angle is approximately \(102^{\circ}\). Therefore, the FOF angle is less than \(104.5^{\circ}\). So, statement B is **correct**.

The diagram shows the \(OF_{2}\) molecule with 2 lone pairs on 'O', a bond angle of \(102^{\circ}\), and a bent/V shape.

Based on the analysis, statements A, B, and D are correct.

questions.question: When 2 litre of ideal gas expands isothermally into vacuum to a total volume of 6 litre, the change in internal energy is J. (Nearest integer)
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The problem states that an ideal gas expands isothermally into vacuum.

For an ideal gas, the internal energy \(U\) is solely a function of its temperature \(T\). It does not depend on volume or pressure.

An isothermal process is one in which the temperature of the system remains constant. Therefore, for this expansion, \(\Delta T = 0\).

Since the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, and the temperature remains constant (isothermal process), the change in internal energy \(\Delta U\) must be zero.

$$
\Delta U = 0
$$

The expansion into vacuum implies that no external work is done (\(W=0\)), but for an ideal gas, the primary determinant for \(\Delta U\) is temperature change.

$$
\Delta T_b = 373.52 - 373 = 0.52 \text{ K}
$$

The formula for elevation in boiling point is \(\Delta T_b = i K_b m\), where \(i\) is the van't Hoff factor, \(K_b\) is the molal elevation constant, and \(m\) is the molality of the solution.

For a non-volatile solute, \(i = 1\).

$$
\Delta T_b = 1 \times K_b \times m
$$

Molality \(m = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{mass of solvent in kg}}\).

Moles of solute = \(\frac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{molecular mass of solute}} = \frac{2}{x}\), where \(x\) is the molecular mass of the solute.

Mass of solvent (water) = 20 g = 0.020 kg.

$$

$$

Given \(\Delta T_b = 0.52\) K and \(K_b = 0.52\) K kg mol\(^{-1}\).

$$
0.52 = 0.52 \times \frac{2/x}{20} \times 1000
$$

$$
1 = \frac{2}{x} \times \frac{1000}{20}
$$

$$
1 = \frac{2}{x} \times 50
$$

$$
x = 2 \times 50
$$

$$
x = 100 \text{ g/mol}

Reaction C shows benzenediazonium chloride reacting with \(Cu_{2}Cl_{2}\) to form chlorobenzene and nitrogen gas. This is a substitution reaction where the diazonium group is replaced by a halogen (Cl), which is characteristic of the Sandmeyer reaction.

Reaction D shows chloroethane reacting with sodium iodide to form iodoethane and sodium chloride. This is a halogen exchange reaction where chlorine is replaced by iodine, which is characteristic of the Finkelstein reaction.

$$
C_{2}H_{5}Cl + NaI \rightarrow C_{2}H_{5}I + NaCl
$$

Thus, D matches with III (Finkelstein reaction).

Based on the analysis, the correct matches are:

• A - II (Wurtz Fittig reaction)
• B - I (Fittig reaction)
• C - IV (Sandmeyer reaction)
• D - III (Finkelstein reaction)

questions.question: 600 mL of 0.01 M HCl is mixed with 400 mL of 0.01 M H$_{2}$SO$_{4}$. The pH of the mixture is $\text{__________}$ \times $10^{-2}$ (Nearest integer) [Given log 2 = 0.30, log 3 = 0.48, log 5 = 0.69, log 7 = 0.84, log 11 = 1.04]
questions.explanation:
The concentration of H\(^{+}\) ions in the final mixture can be calculated by finding the total moles of H\(^{+}\) and dividing by the total volume.

Moles of H\(^{+}\) from HCl = Molarity \(\times\) Volume = \(0.01 \times 600 = 6\) millimoles.

H\(_{2}\)SO\(_{4}\) is a strong acid and provides 2 H\(^{+}\) ions per molecule. Moles of H\(^{+}\) from H\(_{2}\)SO\(_{4}\) = 2 \(\times\) Molarity \(\times\) Volume = \(2 \times 0.01 \times 400 = 8\) millimoles.

Total volume of the mixture = 600 mL + 400 mL = 1000 mL.

The concentration of H\(^{+}\) in the mixture is:

$$
[H^{+}]_{mix} = \frac{\text{Total millimoles of } H^{+}}{\text{Total volume in mL}} = \frac{(600 \times 0.01) + (400 \times 0.01 \times 2)}{1000}
$$

$$
= \frac{6+8}{1000} = \frac{14}{1000} = 14 \times 10^{-3} \text{ M}
$$

Now, calculate the pH:

$$
pH = -\log[H^{+}] = -\log(14 \times 10^{-3})
$$

$$
pH = -(\log 14 + \log 10^{-3}) = 3 - \log 14
$$

$$
pH = 3 - \log(2 \times 7) = 3 - (\log 2 + \log 7)
$$

Using the given values:

$$
pH = 3 - 0.30 - 0.84 = 3 - 1.14 = 1.86
$$

The question asks for the pH in the form \(x \times 10^{-2}\). Therefore:

$$
1.86 = x \times 10^{-2}
$$

$$
x = 1.86 \times 100 = 186
$$

The nearest integer is 186.

questions.question: Formation of photochemical smog involves the following reaction in which A, B and C are respectively. • i. $NO_{2} \xrightarrow{h\nu} A + B$ • ii. $B + O_{2} \to C$ • iii. $A + C \to NO_{2} + O_{2}$ Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The formation of photochemical smog is initiated by the photodissociation of nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) by sunlight.

The first reaction shows NO₂ absorbing energy from sunlight (hν) and breaking down into nitric oxide (NO) and an atomic oxygen (O).

$$
NO_{2} \xrightarrow{h\nu} NO + O
$$

By comparing this with the given reaction \(i. NO_{2} \xrightarrow{h\nu} A + B\), we can identify:

• A = NO (Nitric oxide)
• B = O (Atomic oxygen)

The second reaction shows the highly reactive atomic oxygen (B) combining with molecular oxygen (O₂) to form ozone (O₃).

$$
B + O_{2} \to C
$$

$$
O + O_{2} \to O_{3}
$$

From this, we can identify:

• C = O₃ (Ozone)

The third reaction is \(A + C \to NO_{2} + O_{2}\). Substituting the identified species A and C:

$$
NO + O_{3} \to NO_{2} + O_{2}
$$

This is a known reaction in atmospheric chemistry where ozone oxidizes nitric oxide back to nitrogen dioxide, confirming our assignments.

Therefore, A, B, and C are NO, O, and O₃, respectively.

questions.question: Benzyl isocyanide can be obtained by : A. B. C. D. Choose the correct answer from the options given below :

### Detailed Solution

Benzyl isocyanide can be formed by the following reactions:

When an alkyl halide like benzyl bromide reacts with silver cyanide (AgCN), the major product is an isocyanide. This is due to the predominantly covalent nature of the Ag-C bond in AgCN. The nitrogen atom's lone pair attacks the electrophilic carbon of the benzyl group, forming benzyl isocyanide.

This is the carbylamine test (or Hofmann's isocyanide test), which is a characteristic reaction of primary amines. Benzylamine (\(C_{6}H_{5}CH_{2}NH_{2}\)) is a primary amine. When heated with chloroform (\(CHCl_{3}\)) and aqueous potassium hydroxide (KOH), it forms benzyl isocyanide, which has a distinct foul smell.

• Reaction C involves N-methylbenzylamine, which is a secondary amine. Secondary amines do not undergo the carbylamine reaction.
• Reaction D involves the reaction with potassium cyanide (KCN). KCN is ionic and provides cyanide ions (\(CN^{-}\)). The attack predominantly occurs through the carbon atom, leading to the formation of benzyl cyanide (a nitrile), not an isocyanide.

Therefore, only reactions A and B yield benzyl isocyanide as the major product.

questions.question: Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). **Assertion (A)** : Ketoses give Seliwanoff's test faster than Aldoses. **Reason (R)** : Ketoses undergo $\beta$-elimination followed by formation of furfural. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation:
Seliwanoff's test – Test to differentiate for ketose and aldose.

In this keto hexose are more rapidly dehydrated to form 5-hydroxy methyl furfural when heated in acidic medium which on condensation with resorcinol, as result brown red colored complex is formed.

Assertion (A) is true because ketoses (like fructose) dehydrate faster than aldoses (like glucose) under acidic conditions to form 5-hydroxymethylfurfural, which then reacts with resorcinol to give a red color.

Reason (R) states that ketoses undergo \(\beta\)-elimination followed by formation of furfural. While ketoses do undergo \(\beta\)-elimination (specifically, enolization followed by dehydration), the product for ketohexoses is 5-hydroxymethylfurfural, not furfural. Furfural is typically formed from pentoses. Therefore, Reason (R) is false due to the incorrect product mentioned.

Thus, (A) is true but (R) is false.

questions.question:
The major products 'A' and 'B', respectively, are
'A' $\xleftarrow${$\text{Cold } H_2 SO_4$} $H_3$C-$\underset${$\underset{$CH_3$}{|}$}{C}=$CH_2 \xrightarrow${$\frac{$H_2 SO_4$}{80^\circ C}$} 'B'
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The reaction of 2-methylpropene (isobutylene) with sulfuric acid gives different products depending on the temperature.

At low temperatures (cold conditions), 2-methylpropene undergoes an electrophilic addition reaction with sulfuric acid. The reaction follows Markovnikov's rule.

• Step 1: The \(\pi\) bond of the alkene attacks a proton (H⁺) from H₂SO₄, forming the more stable tertiary carbocation (tert-butyl cation).

$$
(CH_3)_2C=CH_2 + H^+ \longrightarrow (CH_3)_3C^+
$$

• Step 2: The hydrogen sulfate ion (HSO₄⁻) acts as a nucleophile and attacks the carbocation to form tert-butyl hydrogen sulfate.

$$
(CH_3)_3C^+ + HSO_4^- \longrightarrow (CH_3)_3C-OSO_3H
$$

So, product 'A' is tert-butyl hydrogen sulfate.

At higher temperatures (80°C), the tert-butyl carbocation formed in the first step can act as an electrophile and attack another molecule of 2-methylpropene, leading to dimerization.

• Step 1: Formation of the tert-butyl cation (same as above).

$$
(CH_3)_2C=CH_2 + H^+ \longrightarrow (CH_3)_3C^+
$$

• Step 2: The tert-butyl cation attacks a second molecule of 2-methylpropene to form a larger C₈ carbocation.

$$
(CH_3)_3C^+ + (CH_3)_2C=CH_2 \longrightarrow (CH_3)_3C-CH_2-C^+(CH_3)_2
$$

• Step 3: Elimination of a proton (H⁺) from the C₈ carbocation yields a mixture of isomeric octenes. The major product is the more substituted (more stable) alkene, which is 2,4,4-trimethylpent-2-ene.

$$
(CH_3)_3C-CH_2-C^+(CH_3)_2 \xrightarrow{-H^+} (CH_3)_3C-CH=C(CH_3)_2
$$

So, product 'B' is 2,4,4-trimethylpent-2-ene.

Comparing the structures of 'A' and 'B' with the given options, option (2) correctly identifies both major products.

questions.question: A trisubstituted compound ' A ', $C_{10}H_{12}O_{2}$ gives neutral $FeCl_{3}$ test positive. Treatment of compound 'A' with NaOH and $CH_{3}Br$ gives $C_{11}H_{14}O_{2}$, with hydroiodic acid gives methyl iodide and with hot conc. NaOH gives a compound B, $C_{10}H_{12}O_{2}$. Compound 'A' also decolourises alkaline $KMnO_{4}$. The number of $\pi$ bond/s present in the compound ' A ' is
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

We are given the following information about compound 'A' (\(C_{10}H_{12}O_{2}\)):

• Gives a positive neutral \(FeCl_{3}\) test: This indicates the presence of a phenolic hydroxyl (–OH) group attached to a benzene ring.
• Reacts with hydroiodic acid (HI) to give methyl iodide (\(CH_{3}I\)): This is the Zeisel test, which confirms the presence of a methoxy (–OCH_{3}) group.
• Decolourises alkaline \(KMnO_{4}\): This indicates the presence of unsaturation (like a C=C double bond) or an easily oxidizable group. Given the other functional groups, an unsaturated side chain is highly likely.
• It is a trisubstituted compound: This means there are three groups attached to a benzene ring.

Let's assemble the structure from the deduced parts:

• A benzene ring.
• Three substituents on the ring.
• The known substituents are –OH and –OCH_{3}.

The formula of the trisubstituted benzene core with the –OH and –OCH_{3} groups is \(C_{6}H_{3}(OH)(OCH_{3})\), which accounts for \(C_{7}H_{7}O_{2}\). Subtracting this from the molecular formula of 'A' gives the formula for the third substituent, R:

$$
R = C_{10}H_{12}O_{2} - C_{7}H_{7}O_{2} = C_{3}H_{5}
$$

Since the compound decolourises \(KMnO_{4}\), the \(C_{3}H_{5}\) group must be unsaturated. A common example is the allyl group, \(–CH_{2}–CH=CH_{2}\). A well-known compound that fits all these criteria is Eugenol (4-allyl-2-methoxyphenol).

In the structure of Eugenol, we count the π bonds:

• The benzene ring contains 3 π bonds.
• The allyl side chain (\(–CH_{2}–CH=CH_{2}\)) contains 1 π bond in the carbon-carbon double bond.

Total number of π bonds is the sum of π bonds from the ring and the side chain.

$$
\text{Total } \pi \text{ bonds} = 3 + 1 = 4
$$

questions.question: What is the correct order of acidity of the protons marked A-D in the given compounds ?
questions.explanation:
\(H_C\) is the proton of the carboxylic acid group (\(\text{-COOH}\)). On deprotonation, it forms a carboxylate ion in which the negative charge is delocalized over the two electronegative oxygen atoms through two equivalent resonance structures. This strong resonance stabilization makes the conjugate base highly stable. Therefore, \(H_C\) is the most acidic proton.

\(H_D\) is an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen with respect to the carboxylic acid group and is also benzylic. Removal of \(H_D\) produces a carbanion that is strongly stabilized by the electron-withdrawing inductive effect of the adjacent \(\text{-COOH}\) group. Its benzylic position provides additional resonance stabilization through delocalization of the negative charge into the aromatic ring. Because of these combined stabilizing effects, the conjugate base formed from \(H_D\) is more stable than that formed from \(H_A\). Hence, \(H_D\) is more acidic than \(H_A\).

\(H_A\) is the proton of a terminal alkyne. On deprotonation, it forms an acetylide ion in which the negative charge is located on an \(sp\)-hybridized carbon. The high \(s\)-character of the \(sp\)-hybridized carbon makes it more effective at stabilizing the negative charge than an ordinary \(sp^3\)-hybridized carbon. Thus, \(H_A\) is appreciably acidic, but its conjugate base is less stabilized than the conjugate base formed from \(H_D\) in this structure.

\(H_B\) is an \(sp^3\) C-H proton at a carbon that is both benzylic and propargylic. Removal of \(H_B\) gives a carbanion that can be stabilized by delocalization into both the aromatic ring and the adjacent alkyne system. However, this stabilization is less effective than the stabilization available for the conjugate bases formed from \(H_D\) and \(H_A\). Therefore, \(H_B\) is the least acidic proton among the four.

The acidity of a proton increases as the stability of its conjugate base increases. The conjugate base of \(H_C\) is the most stable because its negative charge is delocalized over two oxygen atoms. The conjugate base of \(H_D\) is strongly stabilized by the adjacent electron-withdrawing carboxylic acid group and by benzylic resonance. The conjugate base of \(H_A\) is stabilized by the high \(s\)-character of its \(sp\)-hybridized carbon, while the conjugate base of \(H_B\) receives comparatively weaker stabilization.

questions.question: If P(h, k) be a point on the parabola $x = 4y^2$, which is nearest to the point Q(0,33), then the distance of P from the directrix of the parabola $y^2 = 4(x + y)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation:
The given parabola is \(x = 4y^2\), which can be written as \(y^2 = \frac{1}{4}x\). Comparing this with the standard form \(y^2 = 4ax\), we have \(4a = \frac{1}{4}\), so \(a = \frac{1}{16}\).

A point P on the parabola \(y^2 = 4ax\) can be parameterized as \((at^2, 2at)\). Substituting \(a = \frac{1}{16}\), the coordinates of P are \(\left(\frac{t^2}{16}, \frac{2t}{16}\right)\).

The equation of the normal to the parabola \(y^2 = 4ax\) at \((at^2, 2at)\) is \(y + tx = 2at + at^3\).

Substituting \(a = \frac{1}{16}\), the equation of the normal is:

$$
y + tx = 2\left(\frac{1}{16}\right)t + \left(\frac{1}{16}\right)t^3
$$

$$
y + tx = \frac{t}{8} + \frac{t^3}{16}
$$

Since the point P is nearest to Q(0,33), the normal at P passes through Q(0,33). Substitute \(x=0\) and \(y=33\) into the normal equation:

$$
33 = \frac{t}{8} + \frac{t^3}{16}
$$

Multiply by 16 to clear denominators:

$$
528 = 2t + t^3
$$

Rearrange into a cubic equation:

$$
t^3 + 2t - 528 = 0
$$

By inspection or rational root theorem, we can test integer factors of 528. For \(t=8\):

$$
8^3 + 2(8) - 528 = 512 + 16 - 528 = 528 - 528 = 0
$$

So, \(t=8\) is a root. We can factor the cubic equation:

$$
(t - 8)(t^2 + 8t + 66) = 0
$$

For the quadratic factor \(t^2 + 8t + 66 = 0\), the discriminant is \(D = b^2 - 4ac = 8^2 - 4(1)(66) = 64 - 264 = -200\). Since \(D < 0\), there are no other real roots for 't'.

Therefore, \(t = 8\).

Substitute \(t=8\) back into the coordinates of P \(\left(\frac{t^2}{16}, \frac{2t}{16}\right)\):

$$
P = \left(\frac{8^2}{16}, \frac{2 \times 8}{16}\right) = \left(\frac{64}{16}, \frac{16}{16}\right) = (4, 1)
$$

The second parabola is \(y^2 = 4(x + y)\).

Rearrange the terms to complete the square for y:

$$
y^2 - 4y = 4x
$$

$$
(y^2 - 4y + 4) - 4 = 4x
$$

$$
(y - 2)^2 = 4x + 4
$$

$$
(y - 2)^2 = 4(x + 1)
$$

This is a parabola of the form \(Y^2 = 4AX\), where \(Y = y - 2\), \(X = x + 1\), and \(A = 1\).

The equation of the directrix for a parabola \(Y^2 = 4AX\) is \(X = -A\).

So, \(x + 1 = -1\).

The directrix is \(x = -2\).

The point P is \((4, 1)\) and the directrix is \(x = -2\).

The distance of a point \((x_1, y_1)\) from a vertical line \(x = c\) is \(|x_1 - c|\).

$$
\text{Distance} = |4 - (-2)| = |4 + 2| = 6
$$

questions.question: The minimum number of elements that must be added to the relation $R=\{(a, b), (b, c)\}$ on the set $\{a, b, c\}$ so that it becomes symmetric and transitive is :
questions.explanation:
The given relation is \(R = \{(a,b),(b,c)\}\) on the set \(A = \{a,b,c\}\).

For a relation to be symmetric, if \((x,y) \in R\), then \((y,x)\) must also be in \(R\).

• Since \((a,b) \in R\), we must add \((b,a)\).
• Since \((b,c) \in R\), we must add \((c,b)\).

Number of new elements added for symmetry = 2 (i.e., \((b,a)\) and \((c,b)\)).

The relation now becomes \(R' = \{(a,b), (b,c), (b,a), (c,b)\}\, which has 4 elements.

For a relation to be transitive, if \((x,y) \in R'\) and \((y,z) \in R'\), then \((x,z)\) must also be in \(R'\).

Let's check all possible pairs from \(R'\) and identify missing transitive elements:

• \((a,b) \in R'\) and \((b,c) \in R'\) \(\implies\) \((a,c)\) must be added.
• \((b,c) \in R'\) and \((c,b) \in R'\) \(\implies\) \((b,b)\) must be added.
• \((c,b) \in R'\) and \((b,a) \in R'\) \(\implies\) \((c,a)\) must be added.
• \((a,b) \in R'\) and \((b,a) \in R'\) \(\implies\) \((a,a)\) must be added.
• \((b,a) \in R'\) and \((a,b) \in R'\) \(\implies\) \((b,b)\) (already identified).
• \((c,b) \in R'\) and \((b,c) \in R'\) \(\implies\) \((c,c)\) must be added.

The distinct new elements required for transitivity are \((a,c), (b,b), (c,a), (a,a), (c,c)\).

Number of new elements added for transitivity = 5.

The elements added for symmetry are \((b,a)\) and \((c,b)\).

The elements added for transitivity are \((a,c), (b,b), (c,a), (a,a), (c,c)\).

All these 7 elements are distinct and are necessary to make the relation both symmetric and transitive.

Total minimum number of elements to be added = \(2 \text{ (for symmetry)} + 5 \text{ (for transitivity)} = 7\).

questions.explanation:
Let's analyze statement S1:

$$
S_{1}: ((p \lor q) \Rightarrow r) \Leftrightarrow (p \Rightarrow r)
$$

Since the last column of the truth table for \(S_{1}\) contains an 'F' (in the case where p=F, q=T, r=F), \(S_{1}\) is not a tautology.

Now, let's analyze statement S2:

$$

P (Product of the outcomes is positive) \( = {}^{5}C_{5} \left(\frac{3}{6}\right)^{5} + {}^{5}C_{3} \left(\frac{3}{6}\right)^{3} \left(\frac{2}{6}\right)^{2} + {}^{5}C_{1} \left(\frac{3}{6}\right)^{1} \left(\frac{2}{6}\right)^{4} \)

Where the terms correspond to: All positive, 3 positive & 2 negative, 1 positive & 4 negative respectively.
